subject: Check the pantry. It might help get you through the chaos

Checking your pantry for emergencies might seem alarmist, but recent disruptions show proactive readiness is wise.
Evidence: UK Be Ready campaign, podcast discussion, historical disaster isolation
#DisasterPreparedness #Aletheia

Citizens are urged to stockpile three days of supplies and check pantries to prepare for unexpected major disruptions.

While disaster readiness is sound, articles like this often amplify ambient anxiety rather than structural solutions.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Check the pantry. It might help get you through the chaos

Major disruption is no longer a case of if but one of when. Best prepare for it.

Actual Article Body:

Cut off from the outside world with no power and all roads closed, they were desperate. Not for food or water but for information. When would the roads reopen? How long will we be stuck here? When would electricity be restored - and with it the internet?

Login or signup to continue reading

They wanted to let family members know they were safe. Some had run out of cash. With no internet, there were no ATMs and no eftpos. The mobile signal died when the towers went down.

That intense sense of isolation was palpable the moment we stepped from the vehicle and were swamped with questions, most of which we could not answer.

We'd only made it into town because of our media accreditation. The drive in was scary. Fallen trees littered the road. Smoke made visibility poor. The flashing orange beacon on the roof of the vehicle alerted the fire trucks and tankers to our presence.

Unlike the people isolated in the town, we were able to get home at the end of a very long day. It would be a couple of days before they, too, could leave.

Six years later and towns like Sussex Inlet are better prepared for disaster. Local emergency services have been equipped with solar powered backup and satellite internet links.

But what of the individuals? Are ordinary folk like you and me prepared for the worst nature and, more frequently, hostile actors can throw at us? I know I'm not, which is something I intend to address, thanks to an awareness campaign launched last month on the other side of the world.

The Be Ready campaign urged British citizens to stockpile at least three days worth of non-perishable food, water, first aid kit and medical supplies, torches, batteries, wind-up radios and cash. As ominous as it sounded, it wasn't because of an imminent threat, rather the possibility that some kind of major disruption might occur. And if it did the British government calculated that it might take three days before it could get help to isolated communities.

Must check the pantry, I thought at the time, before a string of distractions kept moving the task further down the to-do list. But listening to Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart on The Rest is Politics podcast on Sunday afternoon moved it up the list...
